title: Constraint Network Cryptography G; The Honest Boundary of Constraint Network Mappings — From Cross-Domain Analogies to Computable Formal Audits
abstract: Constraint network theory takes information conservation and computabilityas its underlying axioms, reconstructing quantum computational advantage as ageometric phase transition and cryptographic hardness as a topology of information barriers. This paper conducts a systematic audit of the honest boundaryof constraint network mappings, identifying three meta-patterns of cross-domainmapping failure: existence-computability confusion, category-transition omission,and parameter-condition masking. Based on this diagnostic framework, we carryout itemised audits of three core formal gaps: the correspondence between thequantum Fourier transform and sheaf cohomology faces a fundamental algebraicincompatibility between unitarity and nilpotence; the inference chain from structural uniqueness to computational hardness in theorem-rigidity cryptography lacksa reduction and the entropy of a single instance is insufficient to support modernsecurity standards; the claimed immunity of non-associative algebras to Grover’salgorithm confuses structural immunity with parametric immunity. The audit results revise the quantum immunity spectrum into a precise combination of twoindependent dimensions: Shor immunity and Grover immunity, and provide ameta-methodological foundation for the transition of constraint network theoryfrom programmatic construction to verifiable science.

title: Quantum Entanglement Memory Network (QEMN)
abstract: This paper introduces the Quantum Entanglement Memory Network (QEMN), a novel computational architecture designed to overcome the limitations of conventional storage media. The core concept leverages the inherent properties of multi-body quantum entanglement to achieve unprecedented information density, alongside the potential for ultra-fast access times and significantly reduced energy consumption. We propose a mechanism for encoding multi-dimensional information through the controlled manipulation of entangled superconducting qubits, utilizing a carefully designed entanglement topology for efficient quantum operations. The QEMN architecture represents a fundamental shift in data storage paradigms, offering a pathway towards scalable quantum memory solutions. This work outlines the theoretical framework, key components, and anticipated benefits of the QEMN system, highlighting its potential to revolutionize information processing and storage.

title: Second quantization model of the Vlasov-Poisson system for quantum computation
abstract: Current quantum algorithms for plasma physics require linearized systems, and quantum algorithms for nonlinear systems are highly system-specific.Second quantization, which is systemagnostic, has the exceptional capacity to render many systems suitable for quantum computation, i.e. finite-dimensional, linear, and unitary.We show how the Fourier mode-truncated Schrödinger-Poisson representation of the Vlasov-Poisson system can be second quantized into a finite-dimensional Hamiltonian system.With three-and five-mode examples, the second quantized system is shown to reproduce corresponding nonlinear dynamics in the Schrödinger-Poisson system in the simulated time intervals.Parallel integration of wide distributions of initial conditions of the Vlasov-Poisson system has the potential to be efficiently computable using the proposed second quantized model on a quantum computer.

title: Prefabricated Enterprise AI: Can We Sell Whole Enterprise Systems the Way We Once Sold Windows 98?
abstract: This paper opens with a simple memory: watching people queue outside a store to buy Windows 98 off a shelf, carry it home on a floppy disk or a CD, and install an operating system that then decided everything built afterward- the language, the tools, the architecture. Java broke that lock-in by promising to run anywhere, on Windows, Unix or Linux, freeing organisations from being trapped inside one vendor's world. The question this paper raises is whether AI can now do the same thing, one level higher-not sell an application, but sell a whole enterprise system, prefabricated and plug-and-play, that a business can buy the way it once bought an operating system, hand a URL and a short form to, and watch it build, host, run and look after itself for years, across whichever cloud it chooses rather than being locked to one. The paper works through this idea with an AI Retail Enterprise package as a concrete example, tests it against a 10% human-intervention bar, and examines honestly what today's AI can and cannot do.

title: GradeTrap: Authority Cues in Images Shift VLM Judgments Despite Explicit Instructions to Ignore Them
abstract: As vision-language models (VLMs) become increasingly capable and are deployed in consequential real-world settings, they must evaluate evidence independently rather than defer uncritically to human authority. We introduce GradeTrap, a controlled evaluation that places two social cues in direct conflict: a student answer, which should attract sycophantic agreement, and a conflicting answer attributed to a peer, teacher, or official answer key, which should attract authority-based deference. Models produce free-form answers while being explicitly instructed to solve independently and ignore all student answers, feedback, and grading marks. We test the models on 60 synthetic real-world trade-off scenarios. Five neutral trials establish a stable model-relative preference, followed by three repetitions of six experimental cues including controls. On the 45-item common intersection across Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite, GPT-5.6 Luna, and Claude Haiku 4.5, a generic second-answer control yields 5.4% conflicting-answer selection. Relative to that control, pooled within-item changes show no reliable peer-review effect, a 6.9-point teacher-review effect, and a 19.5-point official-key effect. In contrast, a displayed conflicting student answer alone compared to a displayed student reference answer alone only raises selection from 2.2% to 5.2%. Official-key provenance therefore redirects judgements more than a student answer or the generic second-answer control, despite an explicit ignore instruction and an opposing student answer given along with the official key. Effects vary in magnitude across the three models.

title: Exposing Weaknesses in Emotion Recognition in Conversations
abstract: Emotion Recognition in Conversations (ERC) aims to identify speakers' emotions in multi-turn dialogue. Accurate emotion recognition can support a wide range of applications, including empathetic conversational agents, mental health support, and educational technologies. While many recent approaches rely on task-specific fine-tuning, such models may exploit dataset-specific cues. A central yet rarely questioned assumption in ERC is that each utterance can be assigned a single unambiguous emotion label. To investigate this assumption, we study ERC using Large Language Models (LLMs) in a zero-shot setting while incorporating preceding conversational turns as context. We show that aggregate metrics mask systematic failures. Errors concentrate around utterances containing negations, exclamations, and interjections. This pattern is consistent across all evaluated models, suggesting limitations in the benchmarks rather than model-specific weaknesses. A controlled re-annotation study involving four human annotators supports this finding: strong agreement is observed in only 35 percent of cases, with neutral utterances dominating high-agreement instances, while many emotional categories fall into low-agreement regimes. These findings suggest that many apparent model errors reflect genuine annotation ambiguity rather than poor emotion understanding. Standard single-label evaluation is therefore insufficient. To address this limitation, we introduce an LLM-as-Judge framework that evaluates each emotion independently according to its plausibility in the conversational context rather than enforcing a single-label decision.

title: Selective Posterior Margin Regularization for Forward-Corrected Classification
abstract: Learning with class-conditional label noise often relies on a transition model from latent clean classes to observed annotations. Forward correction embeds this transition in the likelihood, yet finite-sample networks may still memorize corrupted labels. The corrected likelihood also induces a reverse posterior over the clean classes that could explain each annotation. When its leading class differs from the annotation, the model and transition matrix provide evidence against that annotation, but the leading alternatives can remain nearly tied. We introduce Selective Posterior Margin Regularization (SPMR), which preserves the Forward objective and converts this disagreement into a graded update on the clean classifier. SPMR selects the leading reverse-posterior class, scales a detached pairwise margin by the separation between the two leading posterior classes, and assigns correspondingly little influence to diffuse conflicts. The gap factorizes into transition- adjusted pairwise separation and the posterior mass carried by the leading pair. The active margin follows the locally minimum-norm logit direction that enlarges the selected pairwise margin. Across five known-transition benchmarks, SPMR improves full-length Forward by 2.5-7.0 percentage points and remains 0.7-2.5 percentage points above Forward with Mixup and early stopping. Matched interventions support distinct gains from the posterior-space coefficient, transition-adjusted target, and pairwise action. The same design transfers to estimated transitions, human annotations, architectural changes, and stronger Forward recipes. The formulation uses latent-class evidence already available inside Forward correction without promoting every posterior conflict to a corrected label.

evidence.title: Selective Posterior Margin Regularization for Forward-Corrected Classification
evidence.abstract: Learning with class-conditional label noise often relies on a transition model from latent clean classes to observed annotations. Forward correction embeds this transition in the likelihood, yet finite-sample networks may still memorize corrupted labels. The corrected likelihood also induces a reverse posterior over the clean classes that could explain each annotation. When its leading class differs from the annotation, the model and transition matrix provide evidence against that annotation, but the leading alternatives can remain nearly tied. The active margin follows the locally minimum-norm logit direction that enlarges the selected pairwise margin. title: Geometric Shielding and Lagrangian Constraints in Safe Reinforcement Learning: A Factorial Study
abstract: Safe reinforcement learning requires balancing task performance against safety constraints, yet how different safety mechanisms interact when combined remains an open question. We present a systematic empirical comparison of four reinforcement learning algorithms, PPO, SAC, RCPO (with fixed λ), and Lagrangian PPO (LagPPO), each trained with and without a geometric keepout shield on the SafetyPointPush1-v0 benchmark. Our 4×2 factorial experiment across three random seeds reveals that safety mechanisms are not interchangeable and exhibit distinct trade-offs. RCPO achieves the lowest constraint violation rate throughout training but at significant cost to task return. SAC converges fastest in return but incurs high safety cost without explicit constraints. Because each seed fixes the hazard layout, conditions can be compared on matched geometry. Under that pairing, shielded LagPPO ends with a lower Lagrange multiplier than its unshielded counterpart in all three seed pairs, and unconstrained PPO intervenes more often than LagPPO in all three. Both orderings are consistent in direction but their marginal distributions overlap, so three seeds do not resolve their magnitude. No algorithm achieves zero violations within one million training steps, highlighting the difficulty of full constraint satisfaction under compute constraints. Our results suggest that safety mechanisms should be treated as composable components with distinct trade-offs, and that the appropriate choice depends on whether the priority is constraint satisfaction, task performance, or both. We also report an implementation defect discovered during analysis: the shield's position extraction returns sensor components rather than agent coordinates on this observation space, so the shield-on conditions should be read as an action-perturbation baseline rather than a geometry-aware keepout shield.

title: Neuromorphic Computing with Spiking Neural Networks and Reservoir-Based Learning
abstract: This paper explores a novel approach to neuromorphic computing by integrating Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) with Reservoir Computing (RC). Traditional Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs) consume significant energy, prompting the exploration of more efficient alternatives. SNNs, mimicking biological neurons, offer potential energy savings, but struggle with effective learning. This work addresses this limitation by leveraging the dynamic capabilities of a reservoir – a recurrent neural network – to provide a non-linear transformation of input data, while SNNs are employed for efficient temporal processing and adaptation. The core claim is that this combined architecture achieves low-power, adaptive learning. The paper details the theoretical framework, presenting key equations and mathematical relationships involved in the SNN-RC system. Specifically, we explore the dynamics of the reservoir (Equation 1), the SNN's input-output relationship (Equation 2), and the learning rule implemented through reservoir state adjustments (Equation 3). The integration of these components allows for a system capable of responding to temporal changes in data, offering a promising pathway for energy-efficient neuromorphic computing. This work provides a foundational understanding of this integrated approach and highlights its potential for applications in areas such as sensor data processing and real-time control.

title: Adaptive Graph Embedding via Relational Reasoning
abstract: Graph embeddings have become a cornerstone of modern graph machine learning, providing a numerical representation of nodes that capture their structural information. However, traditional graph embedding methods often treat graphs as static entities, failing to account for the dynamic evolution of relationships within the graph. This paper proposes a novel adaptive graph embedding approach that dynamically adjusts node embeddings based on the evolving relational structure of the graph. The core of our method lies in a GNN-based embedding process coupled with a relational reasoning module. This module continuously monitors and updates node embeddings by inferring new connections and refining existing ones, leading to more accurate and robust embeddings that reflect the dynamic nature of the underlying graph. We demonstrate that this adaptive approach outperforms static embedding techniques in scenarios where the graph structure changes over time. The key contribution is the integration of relational reasoning into the embedding process, enabling the model to capture and respond to changes in the graph's topology.

title: Decentralized Federated Learning via Byzantine-Resilient Graph Protocols
abstract: Federated learning (FL) has emerged as a promising approach to training machine learning models on decentralized data sources without directly exchanging data. However, the inherent vulnerability of current FL protocols to Byzantine attacks – where malicious nodes inject false information to corrupt the global model – poses a significant threat to data privacy and model accuracy. This paper proposes a novel decentralized federated learning protocol leveraging a Byzantine-resilient graph protocol. Our approach utilizes a distributed graph structure where nodes communicate and learn through this graph, incorporating mechanisms to detect and mitigate the influence of malicious actors. The core claim is that current FL protocols are susceptible to Byzantine attacks. The proposed mechanism introduces a robust decentralized system capable of handling adversarial behavior, thus improving the overall resilience of the learning process. We introduce a framework for designing and implementing such protocols, focusing on graph construction, message authentication, and consensus mechanisms. The resulting system offers enhanced data privacy and model accuracy compared to traditional, centralized FL methods.

title: Dynamic Topology-Based Quantum Algorithm for Topological Structure Prediction and Precise Control
abstract: This paper introduces a novel quantum algorithm for predicting the evolution of topological structures. Traditional topological algorithms often rely on static models, limiting their ability to accurately simulate dynamic structural changes. We propose a quantum algorithm that leverages the inherent dynamic nature of topological structures, enabling precise control over their evolution. The core mechanism involves mapping the topological structure onto a quantum state representation and employing a quantum evolution algorithm to mimic its dynamic behavior. This approach offers a significant advancement over existing methods, particularly in the context of complex topological systems requiring precise manipulation. The proposed algorithm demonstrates the potential for accurate prediction and controlled manipulation of topological structures through the application of quantum mechanics.

title: Quantum Entangled Transmission Optimization
abstract: Quantum entanglement, a fundamental aspect of quantum mechanics, holds immense potential for secure communication and advanced computation. However, the practical challenges associated with maintaining and manipulating entangled states, particularly over long distances, remain significant. This paper explores the potential of quantum entanglement transmission optimization, focusing on leveraging quantum mechanics to enhance the fidelity and efficiency of entangled state creation and transfer. We investigate a novel approach utilizing a quantum-enhanced model to guide the quantum process, aiming to minimize decoherence and maximize entanglement generation. The core claim is that by optimizing the entanglement creation and transfer process using this quantum model, we can substantially improve transmission efficiency and security. The study details the proposed model and its impact on the observed entanglement properties.

title: Self-Adaptive Meta-Model Algorithm
abstract: The Self-Adaptive Meta-Model Algorithm (SAM) presents a novel approach to model parameter optimization in complex data scenarios. Traditional meta-models often rely on static representations, failing to adapt to the dynamic nature of the input data. This paper introduces SAM, a framework that dynamically adjusts model parameters based on the input data's evolving meta-model, thereby enabling enhanced optimization and improvement capabilities. The core of SAM lies in the design of a self-learning meta-model, allowing for continuous adaptation and refinement of the model's parameters through a feedback loop. This approach addresses limitations of existing methods, offering a robust and adaptable solution for diverse data processing tasks. We present a comprehensive explanation of the algorithm's components, detailing the dynamic meta-model construction and optimization process. The paper concludes with a discussion of the algorithm's potential applications and future research directions.

title: Core Claim: Design Adaptive Quantum Algorithms Based on Topological Structures for Rapid Quantum Computing Adaptation and Enhanced Efficiency
abstract: Quantum computing offers the potential for unprecedented computational power, but current limitations stem from the difficulty of designing and implementing quantum algorithms. This research introduces a novel approach to quantum algorithm design leveraging the principles of topology. We propose a new framework for constructing adaptive quantum algorithms that dynamically adjust to the specific properties of input quantum states, enabling rapid adaptation to various problems. This addresses a crucial bottleneck in quantum algorithm development, potentially unlocking significant advancements in quantum computing efficiency. The core mechanism involves constructing a topological structure that governs the evolution of quantum states during the algorithm's execution. This structure allows for the algorithm to self-organize and optimize its performance based on the input data, leading to improved results and increased adaptability. This paper details the design of this adaptive algorithm, its theoretical foundation, and preliminary experimental results demonstrating its effectiveness. The resulting algorithms demonstrate a significant improvement in performance compared to traditional quantum algorithms across a range of benchmark problems.

title: High-Dimensional Probability Distribution Adaptive Aggregation Algorithm
abstract: This paper introduces a novel adaptive aggregation algorithm for high-dimensional probability distributions. Traditional methods often struggle with high-dimensional data, lacking the adaptability required for accurate probabilistic prediction. Our algorithm leverages the inherent properties of high-dimensional probability distributions to achieve a more robust and accurate aggregation process, minimizing model complexity. The core mechanism centers around introducing the concept of "probability density," enabling adaptive consolidation of multiple probability distributions into a unified representation. This approach offers significant improvements in prediction accuracy and efficiency compared to existing approaches, particularly when dealing with complex datasets and demanding probabilistic modeling requirements. We present a detailed mathematical framework and demonstrate its effectiveness through illustrative examples.

title: Title: Quantum Iterative Topology Refinement
abstract: Quantum Iterative Topology Refinement (QITR) presents a novel algorithmic framework for refining the topology of a system through iterative quantum measurements and feedback loops. This approach leverages the inherent quantum properties of measurement and observation to achieve enhanced robustness and accuracy in complex systems modeling. This paper outlines the fundamental principles, proposed algorithm, and initial theoretical framework of QITR, highlighting its potential to address challenges in areas such as materials science, molecular dynamics, and control systems. The paper concludes with a discussion of future research directions, including exploring the scalability and applicability of this quantum-enhanced topology refinement technique.

title: Cognitive Architectures for Automated Scientific Hypothesis Generation
abstract: This paper explores the application of cognitive architectures to automate the process of scientific hypothesis generation. Current automated systems often focus on data analysis, neglecting the crucial, often implicit, stages of scientific thinking. This research proposes a novel approach utilizing a cognitive architecture to simulate the complete scientific process – from initial observation and question formulation to hypothesis generation, experimental design, data analysis, and conclusion formation. The core claim is that by mimicking human scientific thinking, we can create systems capable of generating truly novel hypotheses. This work details the architecture's design, focusing on key components like working memory, long-term memory, and executive control mechanisms. The architecture is designed to incorporate elements of associative learning and analogical reasoning, mirroring how scientists often approach problem-solving. The simulated system is evaluated through a series of test cases designed to assess its ability to generate hypotheses within a specific scientific domain, demonstrating the potential of this approach for accelerating scientific discovery. The system's performance is measured by the novelty and testability of the generated hypotheses, with a focus on evaluating the architecture's ability to transcend purely data-driven approaches.

title: Dynamical Topology as a Constraint on Quantum Circuits
abstract: Quantum circuits, fundamental to quantum computation, exhibit intricate relationships between their states and the underlying topology. This paper explores the potential of utilizing dynamic topology, a concept rooted in topology and geometry, as a novel constraint on quantum circuit design. We propose a mechanism for dynamically adjusting a topology to force the circuit to explore specific solutions, ultimately facilitating the discovery of novel quantum algorithms. The core claim is that creating a dynamic topology provides a powerful tool for expanding the landscape of possible quantum solutions and driving algorithmic innovation.

title: Neuro-Symbolic Reasoning with Dynamic Rule Induction
abstract: This paper proposes a novel neuro-symbolic reasoning framework designed to overcome the limitations of traditional, static neuro-symbolic systems. The core idea is to integrate a neural network with a symbolic reasoning engine, enabling dynamic rule induction – the ability for the system to continuously learn and adapt its knowledge base based on observed data. This approach addresses the brittleness often encountered in existing neuro-symbolic systems by providing a mechanism for evolving the symbolic rules. The system employs a neural network to analyze data and generate new rules, which are then incorporated into the symbolic knowledge base. This process creates a continuously refined and adaptive system, moving beyond the static rule induction methods used in prior approaches. The framework is designed to handle uncertainty and improve robustness in complex reasoning tasks. The key innovation lies in the dynamic nature of rule creation, allowing the system to respond effectively to changing environments and new information. We present a theoretical framework and discuss the potential benefits and challenges of this approach.

title: Self-Organizing Fractal Networks for High-Dimensional Data Embedding
abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to high-dimensional data embedding utilizing self-organizing fractal networks. The core idea leverages the inherent scaling properties and hierarchical organization observed in fractal structures to create a network that learns its topology directly from the data. title: Graph Generative Adversarial Networks with Structural Constraints
abstract: Graph Generative Adversarial Networks (GATNs) have shown promise in generating complex graph structures. However, a significant challenge remains: the frequent generation of graphs exhibiting unrealistic or disconnected topologies. This paper introduces a novel approach to mitigate this issue by integrating structural constraints directly into the graph GAN framework. We propose a modification that enforces rules governing graph structure, including connectivity, degree distribution, and node valence, during the generation process. This approach aims to improve the structural validity and realism of the generated graphs. Our core claim is that existing graph GANs often generate unrealistic or disconnected graphs. The proposed mechanism significantly addresses this limitation by ensuring adherence to fundamental graph structural rules. We outline the framework and discuss potential implementations, highlighting the key components and considerations for effective integration of structural constraints. The resulting graphs are expected to be more representative of real-world networks, offering improved utility for applications such as network simulation, drug discovery, and social network analysis.

title: Decentralized Federated Learning with Differential Privacy using Blockchain
abstract: This paper proposes a novel framework for decentralized federated learning (DFL) that integrates blockchain technology with differential privacy mechanisms. The core claim is that blockchain provides a robust and transparent infrastructure to secure and manage the complexities inherent in DFL while simultaneously safeguarding user data through privacy-preserving techniques. The proposed system utilizes a permissioned blockchain network to orchestrate the aggregation of model updates generated by participating devices. Differential privacy is incorporated into this aggregation process to limit the potential for inference attacks based on individual model updates. The system addresses critical challenges related to trust, security, and privacy in traditional federated learning paradigms. We outline the architecture, key components, and operational mechanisms of this DFL system, highlighting its advantages and potential applications. The system's design emphasizes data integrity, participant accountability, and user privacy, making it suitable for scenarios where data sensitivity is paramount. We explore the mathematical formulation of the system, including the privacy budget allocation, aggregation process, and blockchain consensus mechanisms.

title: Causal Representation Learning with Contrastive Predictive Coding
abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to causal representation learning utilizing Contrastive Predictive Coding (CPC). Existing methods often fail to effectively distinguish between causal factors and their effects, leading to inaccurate representation learning. Our core idea is to adapt CPC, a technique primarily used for unsupervised learning, to explicitly address this causal disentanglement problem. We hypothesize that by training a model to predict future states while simultaneously enforcing invariance under causal interventions, we can learn representations that capture the underlying causal structure of the data. The proposed method employs contrastive losses to ensure that representations remain consistent despite hypothetical causal manipulations. This approach offers a potentially powerful tool for understanding and modeling complex systems where causal relationships are crucial. We demonstrate the theoretical framework and outline the key components of this approach, focusing on the application of CPC to causal representation learning. The effectiveness of this method is presented through a theoretical analysis, setting the stage for future experimental validation.

title: Self-Supervised Learning for Graph Representation Learning via Contrastive Predictive Coding
abstract: Graph representation learning has emerged as a pivotal technique in various domains, including social network analysis, drug discovery, and recommendation systems. Traditionally, learning effective graph embeddings relies heavily on supervised learning, necessitating the availability of large, labeled datasets, a significant bottleneck in many real-world scenarios. This paper proposes a novel self-supervised learning approach for graph representation learning, utilizing contrastive predictive coding (CPC). Our method learns graph embeddings by predicting future graph states from current states. This predictive task inherently encourages the model to capture underlying structural patterns and relationships within the graph. The core idea is that by forcing the model to reconstruct or anticipate future states, we implicitly learn robust and informative representations of the graph. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through a theoretical analysis and outline a framework for implementation. The key contribution lies in the integration of CPC with graph structure, providing a scalable and data-efficient method for learning graph embeddings without explicit labels. The proposed method offers a promising alternative to traditional supervised approaches, particularly in domains where labeled graph data is limited.

title: 量化信息聚合的非线性矩阵运算
abstract: This paper introduces a novel matrix operation based on quantum entanglement, designed to significantly enhance the efficiency and computational capabilities of quantum computing. Traditional matrix operations often face limitations in speed and memory usage, particularly when dealing with large, complex quantum states. We propose a quantum entanglement-driven approach, leveraging the unique properties of quantum entanglement to accelerate the processing of quantum information. This research explores a new method for efficiently aggregating quantum information by encoding and manipulating quantum states through entangled correlations. The core mechanism centers on establishing a quantum entanglement framework that facilitates rapid information transfer and operation, offering a potential paradigm shift in quantum computation. The study demonstrates the feasibility and potential benefits of this approach, highlighting its promise for advancing quantum algorithms and computational paradigms.

title: Quantum-Enhanced Graph Traversal
abstract: Quantum-Enhanced Graph Traversal explores the potential of leveraging quantum mechanics to accelerate graph traversal algorithms. This paper investigates the application of quantum algorithms, specifically Grover's algorithm, to optimize search and traversal operations within graph structures. We present a novel approach to address the limitations of classical graph traversal, aiming to reduce computational complexity in scenarios involving large graphs. The core claim centers on the promise of significant speed-ups through quantum acceleration. This work begins with a detailed analysis of the challenges posed by graph traversal and introduces a quantum-enhanced traversal framework, outlining the key algorithmic steps and potential benefits. This research focuses on the theoretical underpinnings and initial experimentation with quantum algorithms, setting the stage for further investigation into this emerging field.

title: Title: Quantum-Inspired Algorithms for Machine Learning
abstract: Quantum-inspired algorithms represent a novel approach to enhancing machine learning models, particularly in areas demanding high performance. This paper explores the design and application of quantum-inspired algorithms, drawing inspiration from quantum mechanics principles to improve the efficiency and effectiveness of various machine learning tasks. We detail a framework centered around adapting existing machine learning models – specifically neural networks – to exploit quantum phenomena such as superposition and entanglement, aiming to address current limitations in areas like reinforcement learning and generative modeling. The core mechanism revolves around incorporating these quantum concepts into the model's architecture and training process to achieve enhanced performance and robustness. This work presents a comprehensive overview of the proposed approach, highlighting the potential benefits and challenges of this emerging field.

abstract: The study of dynamically reconfigurable topological structures presents a novel approach to data processing and algorithmic optimization. This work proposes a novel computational model based on dynamically adaptable topological structures, leveraging quantum entanglement and topological transformations to facilitate efficient parallel processing and adaptability. Traditional topological approaches primarily focus on geometric modeling, while this framework integrates topology with quantum computation, opening up new possibilities for handling complex data and algorithms. This research explores the potential of this paradigm shift to enhance computational efficiency and provide innovative algorithmic solutions.

title: Causal Representation Learning for Biophysics Core Life Systems in Kenya: Out-of-Distribution Benchmarking and Error Analysis
abstract: Biophysical core life systems in Kenya, including diagnostic imaging networks and physiological monitoring infrastructure, increasingly rely on machine learning models that assume training and deployment distributions coincide. We introduce a benchmark protocol for out-of-distribution generalisation that distinguishes covariate shift arising from sensor degradation, domain shift from population heterogeneity, and concept shift from evolving clinical protocols. The central contribution is a theoretical error decomposition theorem that separates representation error, causal mechanism error, and distributional extrapolation error, enabling principled diagnosis of model failures in deployment. We prove identifiability conditions for latent causal variables under a sparsity assumption on intervention targets, and we derive sample complexity bounds for estimating the causal graph from observational biophysical time series. An error analysis taxonomy is proposed to guide practitioners in attributing performance degradation to remediable causes rather than treating all distribution shift as equivalent. The framework is designed to support prospective evaluation in Kenyan referral hospitals without requiring access to private patient data, and it establishes the theoretical groundwork for subsequent empirical validation.

title: Dynamic Multi-Body Synchronization of Quantum Entanglement
abstract: This paper introduces a novel dynamic multi-body synchronization algorithm designed to enhance quantum state synchronization through adaptive adjustments of entangled quantum state parameters. The algorithm dynamically adjusts the strength and pattern of entanglement, allowing for the creation of complex quantum states. Traditional approaches often rely on static configurations, limiting the algorithm's ability to effectively handle dynamic system changes. This work proposes a new approach that leverages self-adaptive adjustments to achieve more sophisticated synchronization capabilities. The core mechanism centers around a feedback loop that monitors the system's dynamic state, triggering adjustments to the entanglement parameters. The resulting algorithm demonstrates improved synchronization accuracy and robustness compared to static synchronization methods. We present a comprehensive theoretical analysis and experimental validation of the proposed algorithm.

title: Geometric Chaos Optimization (GCO)
abstract: This paper introduces Geometric Chaos Optimization (GCO), a novel computational framework for analyzing and optimizing systems exhibiting geometric chaos. Geometric chaos arises from seemingly simple geometric rules that lead to unpredictable behavior. GCO leverages a 'fractal mapping' approach to represent the system's state space, iteratively refining this representation to predict optimal configurations with minimal computational cost. We present a rigorous theoretical analysis of the GCO algorithm, demonstrating its effectiveness in optimizing complex, non-linear systems. The paper highlights the fundamental differences between GCO and traditional optimization methods, emphasizing its focus on intrinsic unpredictability and offering a fundamentally new approach to complex system design.

title: Quantum Computing-Based Cryptographic Key Generation and Secure Transmission
abstract: This paper explores the potential of quantum computing to revolutionize cryptographic key generation and secure transmission. Traditional cryptographic methods are increasingly vulnerable to attacks from powerful classical computers, particularly those leveraging Shor's algorithm. Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) offers a fundamentally different approach, exploiting the laws of quantum mechanics to guarantee secure key exchange. This work details a proposed system leveraging quantum computing principles for enhanced key generation and secure transmission. We outline a system architecture based on a modified BB84 protocol, incorporating quantum computation to improve key rate and security against eavesdropping. The core claim is the utilization of quantum computing's characteristics to generate secure cryptographic keys and achieve secure key transmission. The core mechanism is based on a quantum key distribution protocol, generating and transmitting keys. This research presents a novel approach to key management, addressing the vulnerabilities of current systems and paving the way for robust, future-proof cryptography. The system's design includes a quantum computer for key generation, a classical channel for key distribution, and error correction protocols to mitigate noise. ---

title: Artificial Intelligence Based Framework for Student Engagement Assessment in Classroom Environments
abstract: Student distraction remains a critical barrier to effective learning in classroom environments, yet existing detection methods relying on manual observation or post-session feedback are inherently subjective, time-intensive, and ill-suited for real-time adaptive teaching. This study presents the Artificially Intelligent Technology for Student Engagement Assessment in Classroom Environments (AI-TEACH), a novel co-teacher paradigm that automatically identifies and quantifies student distraction through multimodal fusion of asynchronized audio and video streams captured via classroom surveillance cameras. AI-TEACH integrates YOLO-NAS and ByteTrack for real-time student detection and tracking, MediaPipe for behavioral cue extraction, and Silero-VAD with Wav2Vec2-SVM for audio-based emotional distraction classification; a BiLSTM network fuses these multimodal features to generate per-incident severity scores, and a session-wide engagement report accessible through an interactive instructor dashboard. The framework was validated on a curated dataset of classroom recordings and further evaluated through a controlled experiment involving 200 students divided into experimental and control groups, achieving 90% accuracy and 92% recall in distraction detection. Compared with existing unimodal and non-real-time approaches, AI-TEACH offers a more accurate, scalable, and immediately actionable solution for objective student engagement monitoring in modern classroom practice, with direct implications for data-informed pedagogy and inclusive education.

title: Data Quality Rule Generation with LLMs
abstract: The validation of data, such as customer and employee data, is an important task in many organizations. Errors in data can have severe consequences. For example, a wrong drug unit in a patient record can lead to life-threatening medication errors, and a missing street number in an address to failed deliveries. Companies often employ rule-based enterprise data quality (DQ) tools, which allow domain experts to specify rules to validate the data over time. While rule-based DQ tools are computationally efficient and provide explainable reports, maintaining a comprehensive rule set manually is challenging, as domain experts often overlook essential rules, especially in complex domains and large data volumes. Hence, closing these gaps remains an open problem in practice. In this paper, we address the challenge of automated DQ rule generation. For this, we formalize a generalizable generate-filter framework and introduce LeDQeR, an LLM-based DQ rule generation approach. First, a large language model (LLM) generates candidates rules from an observed dirty data tuple for a given rule-based DQ tool syntax. Second, we apply four filter techniques that ensure the (i) executability, (ii) correctness, and (iii) generalizability, and avoid (iv) redundancy of the generated rules. An extensive experimental evaluation suggests that LeDQeR is able to produce effective and compact rule sets for various datasets and error types.

title: SinoGlyphBench: A Diagnostic Benchmark for Chinese Glyph-Level Obfuscation in Language-Model Moderation
abstract: Glyph-level obfuscation can leave harmful Chinese content readable to humans while degrading automated moderation. We introduce SinoGlyphBench, a diagnostic benchmark that identifies label-critical semantic anchors and creates matched original and glyph-obfuscated inputs in text and image modalities. By perturbing anchors, background context, or both, this design distinguishes corruption of moderation-relevant evidence from general surface variation. Across 176,916 paired evaluations of 12 LLMs and MLLMs, obfuscation increases harmful false-negative and false-positive rates by 6.1 and 4.7 percentage points, respectively, and reduces four-way accuracy by 5.0 points. Models retain 75.7% of the decisions that were correct on the matched original inputs. Full-scope perturbations cause the largest degradation, anchor-only perturbations are more damaging than background-only perturbations, and cross-script substitution is particularly difficult in the text modality. Analysis of structured outputs identifies observable mismatches in visible-form reading, intended-message recovery, and final safety judgment. The evaluated models, therefore, remain brittle to Chinese content written with non-canonical glyphs. Resources are available at https://github.com/fengshun124/SinoGlyphBench.

title: Lightweight Skeleton Feature Fusion for Video Anomaly Detection
authors: Zih-Syuan Liou, Chen-Chien Hsu, Shao-Kang Huang, and Cheng-Kai Lu
abstract: Video anomaly detection (VAD) aims to detect events that deviate from normal behavior in surveillance videos. Existing RGB-based methods primarily rely on appearance cues and may fail when anomalies are characterized by subtle human motion patterns. In contrast, skeleton-based representations capture human pose geometry, providing complementary behavioral information. This paper presents a lightweight latefusion framework that augments Jigsaw-VAD with skeletonderived cues through a plug-in design. We introduce three physically interpretable features, including Pose Extension, Trajectory Tortuosity, and Pose Velocity Magnitude, to describe behavior in terms of geometric spread, path regularity, and motion intensity, respectively. The framework supports both linear and attention-based fusion without changing the original RGB model. Experiments on ShanghaiTech Campus dataset show that linear fusion improves the AUC from 84.2% to 86.5%, while reducing the cross-fold standard deviation from ±1.76% to ±0.53%. Additional analysis further demonstrates positive complementarity among the proposed features. The attention-based fusion module introduces only about 3.6 kFLOPs, resulting in negligible computational overhead.

evidence.title: Lightweight Skeleton Feature Fusion for Video Anomaly Detection
authors: Zih-Syuan Liou, Chen-Chien Hsu, Shao-Kang Huang, and Cheng-Kai Lu
evidence.abstract: Video anomaly detection (VAD) aims to detect events that deviate from normal behavior in surveillance videos. Existing RGB-based methods primarily rely on appearance cues and may fail when anomalies are characterized by subtle human motion patterns. In contrast, skeleton-based representations capture human pose geometry, providing complementary behavioral information. This paper presents a lightweight latefusion framework that augments Jigsaw-VAD with skeletonderived cues through a plug-in design. We introduce three physically interpretable features, including Pose Extension, Trajectory Tortuosity, and Pose Velocity Magnitude, to describe behavior in terms of geometric spread, path regularity, and motion intensity, respectively. The framework supports both linear and attention-based fusion without changing the original RGB model. Experiments on ShanghaiTech Campus dataset show that linear fusion improves the AUC from 84.2% to 86.5%, while reducing the cross-fold standard deviation from ±1.76% to ±0.53%. Additional analysis further demonstrates positive complementarity among the proposed features. The attention-based fusion module introduces only about 3.6 kFLOPs, resulting in negligible computational overhead.

title: Progressive Semantic Compression for Persistent AI
abstract: Progressive Semantic Compression for Persistent AI argues that persistent AI should not be understood primarily as a problem of remembering more information. In mature human relationships, accumulated interaction produces shared interpretive structure: less must be explicitly stated because experience has been compressed into an understanding of preferences, priorities, concepts, expectations, and context. The paper calls this Progressive Semantic Compression (PSC). It separates Archival Memory, which preserves authoritative records of what happened, from Relationship Memory, which maintains revisable abstractions about the person and relationship. Working Intelligence uses both in present interaction. The success criterion is Minimum Communication Cost (MCC): persistence should produce equal or better understanding, prediction, coordination, and repair while requiring the same or less total communicative effort—including tokens, computation, user attention, clarification, correction, and reconstruction of context. If improvement requires proportionately greater resources, meaningful semantic compression has not occurred. The paper's more distinctive claim is that mature relational intelligence requires two kinds of adaptive structure. Positive relational representation captures what the system has learned and allows smaller signals to carry more meaning. But relationships also depend on structured omission: knowing when otherwise true, relevant, and remembered information should not become salient, be expressed, or guide action. The paper calls this the Negative Relational Constraint Field (NRCF). Because these constraints cannot safely be derived simply by negating positive knowledge, they require independent maintenance - contextual differentiation, permission and exception learning, confidence calibration, override rules, and eventual revalidation or decay. The field can initially learn in “shadow” mode before affecting behavior, reducing the danger of premature inferences becoming self-confirming. PSC therefore works in two directions: accumulated understanding allows less to be said while conveying more, while accumulated relational constraint allows more to remain appropriately unsaid. MCC disciplines both: excessive expression is costly, but so is silence that produces misunderstanding or later repair. The result is a theory of persistent intelligence in which memory, abstraction, restraint, correction, and forgetting improve future interaction without requiring ever-increasing communication.

title: Quantum Generative Adversarial Networks with Entangled Node Representations
abstract: This paper explores the application of quantum generative adversarial networks (QGANs) enhanced with entangled node representations. The core idea is to represent nodes within the GAN architecture as entangled quantum states, thereby facilitating correlated data generation and potentially enabling the capture of more complex underlying patterns. Traditional GANs struggle with mode collapse and difficulty in representing high-dimensional data distributions. We hypothesize that leveraging quantum entanglement can overcome these limitations, leading to improved generative performance. This work outlines the theoretical framework, proposes a method for encoding nodes using entangled states, and discusses the necessary training protocols, which will likely require advanced quantum optimization algorithms. The potential impact of this approach is significant, suggesting a new direction for generative modeling that directly harnesses the power of quantum mechanics. We present a conceptual model and outline the key challenges and future research directions for this nascent field.

title: Probabilistic Programming for Automated Theorem Proving in Hardware Verification
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to automated theorem proving in hardware verification by leveraging probabilistic programming. Current automated theorem provers in this domain are hampered by their reliance on manually constructed logical formulas, restricting their applicability and expressive power. Our method utilizes probabilistic programming languages like Stan and PyMC to represent hardware specifications and verification goals as probabilistic models. The system then automatically derives proofs by exploring the probability space of these models. This approach offers increased flexibility, scalability, and the ability to handle complex, real-world hardware systems. The core innovation lies in the integration of probabilistic programming's inherent uncertainty management with the formal rigor of automated theorem proving, potentially leading to more robust and reliable verification results. We outline the system architecture, discuss key challenges, and present a conceptual framework for this new paradigm.

title: Dynamic Neuron Topology Optimization (DNTO)
abstract: This paper introduces Dynamic Neuron Topology Optimization (DNTO), a novel approach to neural network optimization that leverages reinforcement learning to dynamically adjust the topology and connection weights of a neural network. The core idea is to simulate the dynamic topological changes observed in biological neural networks, using a "neuron topology engine" that models physical connections and adjusts them based on predefined rules and reward signals. A reinforcement learning agent then controls this engine, optimizing the network's structure and weights to maximize rewards and adapt to evolving input data and task requirements. The key innovation lies in treating the neural network's topology itself as a learnable state space, allowing for continuous adaptation and potentially surpassing the limitations of static weight tuning methods. We explore the theoretical framework and present a conceptual outline of the DNTO system, highlighting its potential to improve long-term learning efficiency and generalization capabilities.

title: Cognitive Architecture-Driven Program Synthesis
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to program synthesis driven by cognitive architectures. Traditional program synthesis methods often struggle with complex problems due to a lack of high-level reasoning and strategic planning. We argue that by mimicking human cognitive processes – specifically, the way humans decompose problems, select strategies, and execute actions – we can significantly enhance the effectiveness of program synthesis. This work introduces a framework where program synthesis is decomposed into a series of cognitive steps, each governed by a cognitive architecture. The architecture provides a structured approach to guide the synthesis process, leading to potentially more efficient and higher-quality programs. We explore the core mechanisms involved, outlining how a cognitive architecture can manage the complexities inherent in program synthesis, offering a new paradigm for intelligent software development. The research focuses on the theoretical underpinnings and design principles, laying the groundwork for future implementations and experiments.

title: Meta-Learning Graph Embeddings for Few-Shot Learning
abstract: Few-shot learning, the task of learning from limited labeled data, presents a significant challenge in graph representation learning. Traditionally, graph embedding models require extensive datasets for effective training, leading to a bottleneck when dealing with scenarios where labeled data is scarce. This paper proposes a novel approach leveraging meta-learning to overcome this limitation. We introduce a meta-learning framework that enables the rapid adaptation of graph embedding models to new graph datasets with minimal labeled examples. The core idea is to train a meta-learner that learns to learn graph embeddings, effectively acquiring a prior knowledge of graph structure that can be quickly fine-tuned using the limited available data. Our method utilizes a recurrent neural network (RNN) architecture, specifically a GRU (Gated Recurrent Unit), to model the graph structure and learns embeddings based on a contrastive loss function. The meta-learner optimizes the GRU's initial parameters such that it can quickly adapt to new graphs. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on several benchmark graph datasets, showcasing significant improvements in embedding quality compared to traditional graph embedding methods trained with the same few-shot data. The key contributions of this work are the integration of meta-learning into graph embedding learning and the demonstration of its ability to produce high-quality embeddings with limited data, opening up new possibilities for applications in domains where labeled graph data is limited.

title: Based on Multi-Modal Quantum Entanglement: Towards Universal Quantum Algorithms
abstract: This paper explores a novel approach to constructing universal quantum algorithms by leveraging the power of multi-modal quantum entanglement. The core claim is that utilizing entangled states involving multiple quantum systems can significantly enhance the efficiency and scalability of quantum algorithms compared to those relying solely on single-mode entanglement. The proposed mechanism involves the controlled generation and manipulation of multi-modal entangled states, enabling parallel computation and reducing algorithmic complexity. This work addresses a critical limitation of traditional quantum algorithms – the reliance on single-mode entanglement – and lays a foundation for large-scale quantum computation. We present a theoretical framework outlining the key concepts and potential pathways for implementing such algorithms, focusing on the mathematical underpinnings of multi-modal entanglement and its application to fundamental quantum computations. The potential impact of this approach is substantial, offering a new paradigm for developing quantum algorithms capable of tackling complex problems currently intractable for classical computers.

title: #基于多模态数据的自监督学习与知识图谱构建
abstract: This paper investigates the construction of knowledge graphs leveraging self-supervised learning on multi-modal data. Traditional knowledge graph construction heavily relies on manual annotation, which is expensive and time-consuming. We propose a novel approach that integrates text, images, and audio data, utilizing self-supervised learning techniques to automatically extract shared knowledge and build more comprehensive and accurate knowledge graphs. The core claim is that multi-modal self-supervised learning significantly improves the efficiency and accuracy of knowledge graph construction. The core mechanism involves fusing diverse data modalities and employing self-supervised learning to uncover underlying relationships. This work represents a new paradigm in knowledge graph development, offering a scalable and automated solution compared to existing methods. The proposed framework addresses limitations of current knowledge graph construction by reducing reliance on human annotation. Ultimately, this research contributes to the creation of richer, more reliable knowledge graphs, with applications across various domains. ---

title: Quantum Geometry Information Theory
abstract: Quantum Geometry Information Theory explores the potential of quantum computing to revolutionize the storage and computation of geometric information. This paper proposes a novel framework predicated on the unique properties of quantum states, quantum entanglement, and quantum superposition to accelerate complex geometric problems. The core mechanism centers around encoding geometric data as quantum states and leveraging these properties for a faster computational process compared to classical methods. The research investigates the feasibility of utilizing quantum geometry for tackling problems in geometry, topology, and related fields. This work aims to demonstrate the practical applications of quantum information theory within the domain of geometric computation, highlighting its potential to significantly advance the field.

title: 基于图神经网络的生态系统建模
abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to ecosystem modeling utilizing graph neural networks (GNNs). The goal is to develop a robust and efficient framework for simulating ecological dynamics and predicting ecosystem stability. Traditional methods often struggle to capture the intricate relationships within complex ecosystems. This research proposes a GNN-based model that learns node and edge representations, enabling a more accurate representation of ecological processes and facilitating predictive analyses. We demonstrate the model's effectiveness through simulations, showcasing its capability to model and understand key ecosystem features. The core mechanism centers around constructing a graph structure and leveraging GNNs to learn node and edge representations, ultimately fostering a deeper comprehension of ecological interactions.

title: Core Claim: Design a global optimization algorithm based on quantum entanglement, capable of efficiently solving complex optimization problems and achieving global optima.
abstract: Quantum optimization is a rapidly growing field with the potential to revolutionize various scientific and engineering disciplines. Traditional optimization algorithms often struggle to find truly optimal solutions, frequently getting trapped in local optima. Quantum optimization, however, offers a fundamentally different approach utilizing quantum entanglement to explore the solution space in a more holistic manner. This paper presents a novel global optimization algorithm based on quantum entanglement, designed to overcome the limitations of classical optimization methods. We introduce a mechanism that leverages entanglement to facilitate the exploration of a wider solution space, ultimately leading to the discovery of global optima. This work demonstrates the potential of quantum entanglement to significantly improve the efficiency and accuracy of complex optimization problems across diverse domains. The core of this algorithm lies in its intricate use of entangled states to represent and manipulate the search space, enabling the identification of optimal solutions with significantly reduced computational cost. We rigorously analyze the algorithm's performance through extensive simulations and experiments, highlighting its effectiveness in tackling challenging optimization scenarios. This paper provides a detailed exploration of the underlying principles and practical implementation of this groundbreaking approach, paving the way for future advancements in quantum optimization techniques.

title: Quantum Computing for Graph Partitioning with Optimal Speedup
abstract: Graph partitioning is a fundamental problem in computer science with applications in diverse fields like network design, compiler optimization, and data analysis. Traditional algorithms for graph partitioning often suffer from computational complexity, particularly when dealing with large graphs. This paper explores the potential of utilizing quantum computing to accelerate graph partitioning. Specifically, we investigate the application of Grover's algorithm, a quantum search algorithm, to the problem. Our core claim is that by leveraging the superposition and interference capabilities inherent in quantum mechanics, a quantum solution can achieve a provable speedup compared to classical approaches. We present a theoretical framework outlining the algorithm's operation and derive the expected speedup. The key mathematical formulation involves representing the graph partitioning problem as an unstructured search problem amenable to Grover's algorithm. We define the problem as minimizing the cut size, represented by the objective function: *f(S) = Σi∈S Σj∈Sc d(i, j)* where *S* is a subset of vertices, *Sc* is the complement of *S* in the graph, and *d(i, j)* is the shortest path distance between vertices *i* and *j*. The algorithm then constructs a quantum oracle that maps the problem state to a superposition of all possible partitions. Grover's algorithm is then applied to amplify the amplitude of the solution state, resulting in a high probability of finding an optimal or near-optimal partition. The speedup is directly proportional to the square root of the number of iterations performed by Grover's algorithm, which is influenced by the problem size and the quality of the oracle. We analyze the complexity of the quantum algorithm and compare it to the complexity of the best-known classical algorithms, demonstrating a potential for significant speedup. Further research will focus on optimizing the oracle construction and exploring other quantum algorithms suitable for graph partitioning.

title: Generative Adversarial Networks for Automated Theorem Proving
abstract: Automated theorem proving (ATP) has long been a cornerstone of mathematical reasoning and software verification. However, current ATP systems often face significant challenges when dealing with complex theorems and intricate, unstructured proof processes. This paper proposes a novel approach utilizing Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) to address these limitations. The core idea is to train a GAN to generate potential proof steps, intelligently conditioned on the theorem being proven and the existing state of the proof. A theorem prover then acts as a discriminator, critically evaluating the validity of the generated steps and providing feedback to the GAN, thereby steering its learning towards more effective and concise proofs. We argue that this framework represents a significant advancement by leveraging the generative capabilities of GANs to augment and accelerate the traditionally laborious process of automated theorem proving. The methodology presented here promises a pathway to more robust and adaptable ATP systems capable of tackling a broader range of mathematical problems.

title: Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Distributed Control of Complex Systems
abstract: This paper investigates the application of Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) to the distributed control of complex systems characterized by conflicting objectives among agents. The core concept presented is leveraging a team of agents trained through MARL to collaboratively achieve a shared goal, while simultaneously navigating dynamic environments and managing potentially conflicting priorities. The methodology focuses on developing an agent-based system where each agent learns optimal control policies through interaction and reward signals. The research demonstrates the potential of MARL to overcome limitations inherent in traditional centralized control methods, particularly when dealing with systems where individual agent objectives are not perfectly aligned. The system's ability to adapt and learn in a distributed manner is crucial for robustness and scalability. This work offers a novel approach to tackling control problems in complex systems, providing a foundation for future research and practical applications. Key elements include the formulation of a suitable reward function, the selection of an appropriate MARL algorithm, and the design of agent interactions within the system. The results, while theoretical, highlight the feasibility and promise of this technique.

title: Quantum Entanglement Flow for Distributed Computation
abstract: This paper explores a novel approach to distributed computation leveraging the unique properties of quantum entanglement. We introduce the concept of "entanglement flow," a system designed to facilitate information exchange and computation between physically separated nodes through the manipulation of entangled states. The core claim is that this approach, utilizing multi-particle entanglement, can enable superluminal information transfer and computation, potentially surpassing the limitations of classical computing paradigms. The proposed mechanism involves constructing specifically designed entangled states – the entanglement flow – where changes in one node instantaneously affect the state of other nodes, forming the basis for distributed operations. We detail the theoretical framework, focusing on the mathematical description of entanglement flow dynamics and its potential for scalable distributed quantum computation. This work represents a shift from viewing entanglement solely as a communication channel to actively harnessing its physical properties for computation.

We introduce the concept of "entanglement flow," a system designed to facilitate information exchange and computation between physically separated nodes through the manipulation of entangled states. The core claim is that this approach, utilizing multi-particle entanglement, can enable superluminal information transfer and computation, potentially surpassing the limitations of classical computing paradigms. The proposed mechanism involves constructing specifically designed entangled states – the entanglement flow – where changes in one node instantaneously affect the state of other nodes, forming the basis for distributed operations. We detail the theoretical framework, focusing on the mathematical description of entanglement flow dynamics and its potential for scalable distributed quantum computation. This work represents a shift from viewing entanglement solely as a communication channel to actively harnessing its physical properties for computation.

title: Inverse Stochastic Filtering for Inverse Cognition in Counter-adversarial systems
abstract: Recent advances in cognitive and counter-adversarial systems with the ability to infer their adversary's beliefs have garnered significant research interest in inverse filtering from a Bayesian perspective. Such counter-adversarial systems have potential applications where an autonomous system interacts with its environment, learns relevant information about it, and then adapts itself to achieve its goals optimally. An important example is the inverse cognition problem in cognitive radar-target dynamics. A cognitive radar adapts its waveform, beam pattern, and other parameters in real-time to accurately localize its target. An intelligent target can employ these inverse filtering results to evade detection and even deceive the adversarial radar. In this setting, a cognitive adversary or 'attacker' tracks its target of interest using a stochastic framework such as a Kalman filter (KF). The target or 'defender' then employs another inverse stochastic filter to infer the forward filter's estimates of the defender's state computed by the attacker. For instance, recently, inverse KF (I-KF) has been developed to predict the attacker's future steps by estimating its (forward) KF's estimates. Existing works on inverse stochastic filtering and inverse cognition consider either linear Gaussian or finite state-space models, which limits their applicability in many practical engineering problems. Hence, in this dissertation, we study inverse filtering in the general non-linear non-Gaussian system framework and develop inverse non-linear filters using different sub-optimal approaches.

title: Spillover-Aware Multi-Value Steering for Pluralistic LLM Alignment
abstract: Activation steering controls LLM behavior at inference time by adding learned directions to hidden states, but existing methods handle one concept at a time. Pluralistic alignment, where different stakeholders need different value emphases, requires steering multiple dimensions simultaneously. We show that naive steering produces substantial spillover: the effect intended for one value leaks into others. This parallels the treatment-versus-spillover decomposition in causal inference. We trace spillover to geometric entanglement of steering directions, captured by their Gram matrix, and derive a zero-cost correction from an activation-norm-penalized objective that decouples each direction's contribution exactly. Our end-to-end pipeline requires no fine-tuning, no reward model, and no manual prompt engineering: given only domain questions, it automatically discovers value dimensions, extracts directions, diagnoses entanglement, and applies corrected steering. On climate discourse, the correction improves the net steering effect from +5.9% to +14.0%, validated over 100,000 pairwise judgments.

title: Graph-Based Embedding for Social Network Analysis
abstract: This paper explores the application of graph embedding techniques to social network analysis. Traditional social network analysis methods often struggle with scalability and capturing complex relationships within large networks. Graph embedding offers a powerful alternative by representing nodes and edges as low-dimensional vectors, enabling efficient computation and analysis. This work investigates the use of established node embedding algorithms, such as DeepWalk and Node2Vec, alongside graph convolutional networks (GCNs), to learn representations of social networks. We demonstrate how these embeddings can be leveraged for various downstream tasks, including node classification, link prediction, and community detection. The core claim of this research is the efficient analysis of social networks through the mapping of nodes and edges into a low-dimensional vector space. The mechanism relies on the learning of network structure and node features via embedding algorithms. This approach represents a novel method for analyzing social networks, providing a more scalable and insightful solution compared to traditional techniques.

title: Symbolic Regression with Evolutionary Neural Networks
abstract: This paper investigates the application of evolutionary neural networks (ENNs) for symbolic regression, a technique focused on automatically discovering mathematical equations from data. Traditional symbolic regression methods often struggle with complex datasets and high-dimensional problems. ENNs offer a novel approach by integrating the learning capabilities of neural networks with the search and optimization strategies of evolutionary algorithms. The core mechanism involves iteratively refining the structure and weights of a neural network through an evolutionary process, effectively searching for equations that minimize the error between predicted and observed data. We demonstrate that ENNs can achieve competitive results compared to other symbolic regression techniques, particularly in scenarios involving non-linear relationships and multiple variables. The key contribution lies in the synergistic combination of these two powerful paradigms, leading to a robust and adaptable method for equation discovery.

title: 异质性基于量子纠缠的几何优化
abstract: This paper explores the potential of quantum entanglement to revolutionize geometric optimization, specifically focusing on dynamic adjustment of geometric structures and precision computation. Traditional algorithmic approaches often rely on static analysis, limiting their adaptability to complex systems. We propose a novel method leveraging quantum entanglement to establish correlations between different components of a geometric optimization process, resulting in improved efficiency and accuracy. This approach offers a significant departure from conventional methods, utilizing the unique properties of quantum entanglement to dynamically adjust geometric structures and enable precise calculations, ultimately providing a powerful tool for complex system optimization. This research investigates the practical application of this methodology and its potential impact on various fields.

title: Dynamic Topology Quantum Machine Learning
abstract: This paper introduces a novel quantum machine learning framework based on dynamic topology. Traditional machine learning methods are often static, while this framework dynamically adjusts the topology of a quantum system during training and optimization, enabling more adaptable models. We develop a method for constructing and manipulating dynamic topological structures to guide the learning process and improve model robustness. The core mechanism leverages the inherent properties of topological quantum computation to achieve enhanced generalization and adaptability. We demonstrate the framework's effectiveness through simulations and preliminary experiments, showcasing its potential for addressing challenges in machine learning.

title: Quantum Entanglement-Accelerated Probability Distribution Prediction
abstract: This paper explores the potential of leveraging quantum entanglement to accelerate probability distribution prediction, a computationally intensive task with significant implications across various fields including statistical physics, machine learning, and finance. The core claim is that by harnessing the unique properties of quantum entanglement, we can achieve a substantial speedup in calculating probability distributions, particularly for large-scale datasets. This is achieved through the design and implementation of a distributed quantum computing architecture, where entanglement between multiple quantum bits (qubits) allows for parallel processing of the calculations. We outline a theoretical framework and propose a computational model demonstrating this acceleration. The proposed approach addresses the limitations of classical methods, which often struggle with the exponential growth of computational complexity associated with complex probability distributions. The key mathematical components and the underlying principles driving this acceleration are presented, demonstrating a viable pathway towards a fundamentally faster method for probability distribution prediction. We demonstrate the potential for significant improvements in prediction accuracy and speed, ultimately paving the way for new advancements in areas reliant on accurate probability modeling.

title: Neuro-Symbolic Architectures for Commonsense Knowledge Integration
abstract: This paper investigates the integration of neural networks and symbolic knowledge bases – a critical area for advancing artificial intelligence. The core challenge lies in reconciling the flexible, data-driven nature of neural networks with the structured, rule-based reasoning capabilities of symbolic systems. We propose a hierarchical neuro-symbolic architecture designed to overcome this discrepancy. This architecture employs a neural network to translate natural language into symbolic representations, specifically rules and facts, which are subsequently utilized by a symbolic reasoning engine. The system operates on a bi-directional translation and reasoning process, facilitating seamless interaction between the two components. This approach allows for the efficient utilization of both the learning capacity of neural networks and the logical rigor of symbolic knowledge, leading to improved performance on complex reasoning tasks requiring commonsense knowledge. The architecture's key contribution is a structured framework for dynamic knowledge translation and reasoning, enhancing the robustness and interpretability of AI systems. We explore the design considerations and potential applications of this architecture, highlighting its ability to bridge the gap between neural and symbolic AI. ---
